"Eponymous" is an adjective that describes a naming relationship — specifically, the connection between a name and the thing that carries it.

Whenever something (a book, a film, an album, a city, a company) is named after a particular person or entity, the word "eponymous" is used to highlight that connection.

That's it at the core. But to truly own this word, you need to understand the two directions it works in.

Direction 1 — Describing the person (or thing) that gave the name

When a person is the source of a name — meaning something out there is named after them — that person can be called "eponymous."

"Romulus, the eponymous founder of Rome."

This means: Rome is named after Romulus. He is the source of the name. He is the eponymous one.

"Jerry Seinfeld is the eponymous star of the show Seinfeld."

The show carries Jerry's name. He gave his name to it. So he is described as eponymous.

"Walt Disney lent his name to the eponymous entertainment empire."

Disney (the company) is named after Walt Disney (the man). Walt is the eponymous figure.

Direction 2 — Describing the thing that is named (especially self-titled works)

"Eponymous" also works in the other direction: describing something that shares the name of its creator or main subject.

This is extremely common in music journalism:

"The band released their eponymous debut album."

This means the album is named after the band itself. If a band called Coldplay releases an album titled Coldplay, that is their eponymous (or "self-titled") album.

It's equally common in literature and film:

"Emma is the eponymous heroine of Jane Austen's novel."

The novel is called Emma. The character's name is Emma. The character and the title share the same name. Emma is therefore the eponymous heroine.

Other clear examples:

  • Hamlet → Hamlet is the eponymous prince.
  • Forrest Gump → Forrest Gump is the eponymous character.
  • Frankenstein → Victor Frankenstein is the eponymous scientist.
The Key Insight: Two Ends of the Same Relationship

These two uses are not actually different meanings — they are simply two ways of describing the same relationship, depending on which end you're pointing at.

Think of it like a bridge between two things: a person's name and something named after them. "Eponymous" can describe either end of that bridge.

  • Point at the person → they are the eponymous figure (they gave their name).
  • Point at the work/thing → it is eponymous (it carries their name).

Both are correct. Both appear in real writing. You just need to read the sentence carefully to know which end is being described.

In literature and film: Any character whose name is also the title of the work is an "eponymous character." If the character's name is NOT the title, they are not eponymous — no matter how important they are. (Elizabeth Bennet, for instance, is the protagonist of Pride and Prejudice, but she is not eponymous, because the title is not her name.)

In music: A self-titled debut album is almost universally called an "eponymous album" by critics and journalists. It's one of the word's most frequent habitats.

In history and mythology: Legendary or historical figures who gave their names to cities, countries, tribes, or eras are called eponymous.

  • "America" is believed to be named after the explorer Amerigo Vespucci, making him the eponymous explorer.
  • The "Hermitian matrix" in mathematics is named after Charles Hermite — he is its eponymous mathematician.

In business: Companies named after their founders are often described as eponymous.

  • "She built an eponymous fashion brand." (The brand carries her name.)

This is important. "Eponymous" carries one and only one meaning: it is always about a name being shared or given. It does not mean:

  • Famous
  • Important
  • Original
  • Self-made

A character is only "eponymous" if they share their name with the title of the work. A founder is only "eponymous" if the company or place bears their name. The word has nothing to do with greatness or significance on its own.
A Simple Test Before Using It

Before using "eponymous," ask yourself: Is there a name that belongs to both the person and the thing being described? If yes — if a name is shared or transferred from one to the other — then "eponymous" is the right word.

Since you'll encounter this in the wild, it's worth knowing: the noun form is "eponym." An eponym is the person (or thing) whose name is given to something else. Romulus is the eponym of Rome. Amerigo Vespucci is the eponym of America. The adjective "eponymous" is simply the describing word built from this noun. You don't need to use "eponym" actively, but recognizing it will help you understand "eponymous" even more solidly.
